segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We’re glad you came to visit us. What we’re doing here, for the students to learn from and if you want to hear your talk, that’s why they are saving these. Whenever you want to listen to your interview, you can do it any time, also the kids/students.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what we’re gonna do now. What is your name in English?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Roy Grimmett.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Adakeheg(a).

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Adakeheg(a). Where did your name come from? Who named you?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I don’t really know, because when I was nine years old my mom passed away. And my dad passed away when I was 11. Until later, my older brother was telling me things. That’s the only time I learned things.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: My dad’s name was Yon(a) and Mom’s was Tsigonel(i).

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And in English?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Bear Grimmett, Elisa Grimmett.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How many kids were there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: At the beginning, there were nine. Two died when they were real young, I don’t know why. The seven of us, there are four boys and three girls. We all grew up together.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where did you all grow up?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Bunch-i and Greasy – Go-i.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that where you all went to school?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, Cave Springs and Greasy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you all finished at Greasy you went to Cave Springs. Did you all graduate?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I did, but the others didn’t.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who is the eldest?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: George Grimmett – Diganiyisg(i) is his Cherokee name.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t think I ever knew him. And the next one was Turner, then Rufus, and I forgot the girls’ names.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: The girls: Linda, Roberta, and Louise. I don’t know their Cherokee names.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you all started school, were you speaking English or Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I was just telling someone this. I was six years old before I could start school. And when I went, I didn’t know one word of English. Do you remember Reece Fry? That old (woman) teacher.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She probably had already left.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: She was the one that whupped me because I didn’t understand what she was saying. I didn’t understand any English.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How old were you when you started speaking English?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Probably when I was around seven, I started learning it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You learned it quick, didn’t you?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I’m still learning.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They didn’t keep y’all from speaking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Not really there…but they did at Gore. Have you heard of Nochitown?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s where we moved to, and there was a [sick?] family, my brother and sisters we had to talk English there. We had to say, “No, sir. Yes, sir.” We couldn’t say, “Uh-uh” or “Yeah.” If we did say that then we got in trouble.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And when we ate lunch, what all was ‘in’ the plate we had to eat it all up. There were things I didn’t like.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But you had to eat it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That really was hard on me. There would be just me and the teacher sitting there. The others had already gone outside. “Eat!…Eat!” the teacher was telling me. “I can’t! I don’t like it!” I told them. Then the others started feeling sorry for me. So as soon as we got into the lunch room, they would take the food I didn’t like and wrap it up in a paper. Or they’d put it in their pockets. And also, they would put it in their plate just cause they were helping me. When you eat all your food, then they gave you ice cream.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You probably didn’t like that either! [laughs]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: One time…we just lived nearby, but she wouldn’t let me go home to eat. One time, I was thinking, “Boy, what am I going to do?” It was right before lunch. I hid, and then I went out. There was a big tree. I climbed it and got on top of the roof. That’s where I was hiding, and I saw the teacher come out looking for me. And she found me, too. I came on down and we went to the lunchroom. We sat there for a long time. Hudson is my oldest brother’s name. We were telling and telling him about it. He also felt sorry for me. So, we just came back to Greasy. Back at home, we came back to where we had left from. It was a good place. You could do anything you want.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How long did you all live over there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Not even a year. Have you heard of Utsilv – Cotton. They were farming at that time at Webbers Falls. We were working over there, I was just little when I was helping them. My brother Hudson, his wife, and I. We were making $6 to $8 a day. A row of cotton, they were planted a mile long. That’s all it was, $2 a day. I enjoyed it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did they feed you all? Or did you have to buy your own food?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: We would get it ourselves from the store.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all were working hard, weren’t you?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, we really were. I don’t guess you remember that I was born in ’44. Me, I remember when I was growing up things were really hard. Shoes, clothes, they wouldn’t give it to you just any time. It was just like the food stamps. I don’t know how often it was, or if it was once a month. When we got those, that’s when they bought socks or shoes for us, or coats. It was really hard times.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How much were the vouchers you all got to buy this stuff with?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I don’t know, they might’ve been $85.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: For the month?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. When I was in 11th grade, I still didn’t really have any clothes. But the others I saw, they were wearing good clothes. I thought, “Boy, look at the old clothes I got on.” I was 17, I quit the 11th grade.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You didn’t graduate?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: For a month, I didn’t go to school. And they had people that watched school records. The teachers, my teacher, came to the house and they were asking why I quit school. I told them everything. “I don’t have clothes,” I told them. That’s why I quit school. “I don’t have no clothes,” I told them. They went and talked about it. “What if we help you? If we give you a check every month, can you go get clothes and go back to school?” “Yeah!” I told them. Cause I like to learn. “I’ll go back, but not right now. I have to get clothes before I go,” I told them. So, not even a month, I got a check. A pair of Levi’s was $3 back then. $3 for a pair of Levi’s. I was really wearing good clothes then.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then you felt better!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Especially now we were finding boyfriends and girlfriends.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You started flirting!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: It was still dark [in the morning] when I was waiting for the bus.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You really liked to go to school.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. You don’t remember my grandma lived way down the hill?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Where our cemetery is, way down at the end of the hollow. That’s where we lived. We had to walk a mile to catch our school bus.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did Hudson raise you all?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, he raised us.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn’t realize he was that old.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I’ve heard that I was only 18 when my parents died.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So, he really was the eldest. I thought you all were closer together [in age].

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: The youngest, my little sister, she was just two years old. I had seen Hudson and Maine Turner cooking.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So Hudson wasn’t married?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ohh!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: But finally, he said he was going to ask somebody to help raise us, they said. Then he, himself, was telling me they separated us cause nobody wanted to help him raise us. Then finally one said, “OK, I’ll help you. I will start helping you,” she said. Really, I understood the name, the same as my mom. Tsigonel(i) was her name. And he brought a woman with the same name. She was really good to us and raised us. Doing things for us; cooking, washing our clothes, and getting us ready for anything. When we all grew up, all became adults, and they split up. I don’t know. But he found another woman, my brother. And the old lady, she stayed by herself until she died. And all the children, they called her “Granny.” Even today, when they talk about her, they say “Granny.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess they really loved her.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where were you all born?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Where were we born?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Where we was born? Oh, I was born at home in Bunch, they said. Let me tell this, I had a hard time getting my birth certificate. Just because I was born at home.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It is hard to get one. My dad barely got one.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What do they call it? “Delayed birth certificate.” That’s what happened to my dad, too.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Did you know Ulogil(i)’s daughter, Tsigeyu? Leslie.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, yeah! We are close kin, we talk all the time.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Where does she live now?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Broken Arrow.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Just for a little while, we were friends. We were in the same grade. When we graduated, we both decided to go somewhere. She was going to California, but I was having problems getting my birth certificate. I couldn’t get it. I still remember, there was a “passenger train” – “people could ride it” they called it, in Stilwell. The train came, we were there, Ulogil(i), his wife and An(a)le. We all took Leslie there when she left.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What was the reason why you all were going there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: To go to school.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh! I think she talked about that. Didn’t she go to learn to be a nurse?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I forgot. But I was going for printing.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I think I’ve heard her talk about that before. You were unable to go with her.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, I haven’t seen her since.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, she lives there. It’s been a while since her husband died.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Her sister, Juanita, passed a few months ago. Did you know her?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah! Robert, their brother, was telling me about that. He said he only had one sister left. They were close in age, Leslie and my sister Linda. That’s how I know about Leslie marrying a man from a different tribe. They met somewhere.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He came from somewhere. Yeah. I forgot, how would you say his tribe was? She talked about it before, Leslie.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: She didn’t have kids?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, she had two boys. One passed away last year.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Mm.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The older one passed. And there’s a grandchild living. She’s really nice, isn’t she?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We talk almost all the time.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Boy. When she left, boy it hurt me. My children, I have two boys and two girls. But they’re all grown now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How many grandkids do you have?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Over 100. [laughs]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really? I’ve never heard of anybody having that many.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: My eldest son’s name is Roy Lee. The other boy’s name is Marco. Diane, and I forget the other one now … Victoria! She’s the youngest.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How many kids do they have?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Diane just has two. Victoria, also, has two. And Marco, the youngest boy, he has three. Roy Lee has nine.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do your kids speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: No! Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And their kids don’t either?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I’ll tell you… since my wife left, we don’t speak Cherokee at the house. Because…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: …you don’t have anybody to talk to in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I have five stepdaughters. And they all speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do they teach their kids?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s what they say, but none of them speaks.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: [laughs]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s funny. I just don’t know what to say. I still remember the way my grandpa talked. I still remember the old Cherokee. But I’ve forgotten a lot of it. That’s what I say, I don’t hear it anymore. The same as the Creek [language], I knew a good amount, but I have forgotten it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Which one of you all was Creek?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Mom.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She spoke good Cherokee and Creek?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: My grandma. Haya was her name. Wane(i) was my grandpa’s name. That’s why they have Hickory Vann Hollow written on the cemetery.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where you all grew up, did you all have radio?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Uh huh, but the battery was this [gestures] long and this [gestures] thick.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what a lot of people said.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And the record player. Ditlod(i) – (set on top of) they called it. You had to sit by it, and do this [gestures].

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Itself…

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: But the one we had was broke. You had to use your finger to make it spin. As long as you were doing that, you could listen to the music.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you all take turns doing that?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: T.V. –television—we were already grown, the late Digal(i)sd(i), he lived by railroad tracks. And we lived up on the hill. A bunch of us, we walked down the hill in the evening. We came to Digal(i)sd(i)’s house to watch T.V. Digal(i)sd(i), he was working on the railroad. Up above the T.V. he had a note: “Lights out at 10 o’clock!”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s when you all were supposed to leave!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: When that time came, right then, we had to leave.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did they run you all off? [laughs]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And we started walking, talking and laughing all the way up to the house. Not until we all were grown, did somebody get a T.V. What do they call a T.V. in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Didayvlatvsg(i).

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Didayvlatvsgi, yeah, that’s what they called it. It was just black and white, for a while.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was there a lot of you that got together to watch T.V.?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Our neighbor, we hadn’t seen each other for a while, they came. [laughs] Back then, there was real love here.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Real love. They really showed love when people saw each other.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They visited each other, too! Didn’t they?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, they visited each other.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about--…go ahead, finish [what you’re saying].

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I’m saying, nowadays something will happen next door and you’ll know nothing about it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Or they won’t talk to you.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, they don’t talk to you. It really is a bad time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about things to play with? What did you all have? Nowadays, kids have a house full of toys.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: My plaything was tires. Rubber tires. We would push them around. And then there was Uyut(i). Wagon—Dogwalela—wagon. It's in the middle.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: A hub-ring?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, when I would find that, that was great. And then wire, baling-wire, I would make it long and tie it to it. And I would drag it around. All in the woods I had little trails to drag it around. If I didn’t have that, then there was a creek nearby where we swam. Also, I just thought about what we was talking about a while ago. My older sister, I didn’t really see her. She swam too long in the hot sun, and her head got too hot. Then she started having a nosebleed for good. That’s what killed her. She was the eldest and the first to pass away.
Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Well that must’ve been really hot, for that to happen.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: This road right here, that’s about how far it was to the water, we would swim. And there was a spring there, it was good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you all get water there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Oh yeah!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s where you all drew water.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. And when they washed, I was using two buckets. Back then, they used to heat up the water.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh. They built a fire, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. I had to look for all the wood. And then build the fire. And then I would fill up the pot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s where they’d put all the white clothes. I remember Grandma used to do that. The water that she put the clothes in was really hot. And she also added something. They didn’t do that?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. Also, I helped--[phone goes off] Haw! – Hey!
(on phone) Hey! Are you home?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: No, I’m at the office. Talking—talking Cherokee—talking Cherokee.
(on phone) OK, bye-bye.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: OK, bye. That was Diane, that I mentioned, my oldest daughter. But also, when they made soap, I helped.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I never...

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Lye! Lye soap, they called it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: My old aunt, her husband’s name was Grimmett. Ellis, you might’ve known them.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Ellis?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Ellis – Diyotl(i) was his name.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah! That was my dad’s brother.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, Yon(a) – Bear Grimmett – Ellis Grimmett.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, is that right?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, they grew up in Tailholt.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: The boys, they were all short. Dutch…

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah! Dutch, Dick, Ray, Turner… haw, I forgot what their name was. He’s the one that made the soap. They’d chase you off if you came too close to the boys. “Y’all get out of here. You don’t have any business here. Y’all just get out.” I don’t know why they were doing that. There were a few different people that said the same thing happened to them. If you come close to the boys, they’ll chase you. They were making that kind of soap. I don’t know why they were doing that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it bitter?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Huh-uh. If the boy came too close, things broke. They used to say.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Ray is the only one living now.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, he’s the only one.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, the same … when they planted a garden, they said, “If you’re chewing gum, huh-uh, you can’t come in [the garden.]”

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s how it was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Hm. I never heard that.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I have heard a lot of things like that.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: And I still believe it, too.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: They wouldn’t let us bring food [from outside] to the garden.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Another thing, like a pregnant woman, they had a lot of rules for her. One, she was not supposed to stand in the doorway. Or stand by the window. “Huh-uh, huh-uh!” they would say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “Don’t be looking out!” they would say. If you looked out, “Don’t be doing that,” my grandpa would say.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: There’s a lot that we don’t live by anymore.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I don’t know why, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you all live in a big house?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Huh-uh! It was a real small house. It had two bedrooms, a kitchen, and a living room.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was there a bed there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: They had one bed and the rest of us slept on the floor. It was leaking when it rained. I remember, they used to wake us up and move us while they would put buckets down. And then it’d be…[drip]…[drip]…[drip] [laughs]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then it was hard to sleep!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I had to listen to it. It was funny, it’d be alright if it was half of the problem, I think nowadays. The children are growing up lazy. They’re lazy. They don’t know anything. They don’t even know how to cut wood. I used an axe, and had a big pile of wood.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You cut wood.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I used an axe to cut them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How about with cooking? What did they use?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Wood.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The wood that you cut?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah! They had to be cut real small for the stove. I did that and I wasn’t even lazy. I liked it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ooh! The food is really good cooked by the wood stove.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Boy, yeah. It is good cooked that way. One stepdaughter, her name was Frankie. Where she lives, it’s like this. And right by there, they built a little building, just one room. And that is where she cooked. She got a cook stove like that, and that’s where she cooks all the time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I got one, too, the one my grandmother used. I cook there, too, sometimes. It is really good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You knew my grandmother, Ged(i) – Katy Pritchett.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was my dad’s mom.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, Ged(i) I knew her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was her brother, Ulogil(i).

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That was her brother?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ulogil(i), that was her brother.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: How about Mack Brewer, do you remember him?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mack Brewer?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I knew them, Mack Brewer. We worked together at Old Ft. Smith.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Me too, Ft. Smith, too. Dave Sanders, also, Mack, there were about four of us, we were working together. Mack and I were kinfolk. He used to live in Markoma. It must be about four years ago now, Greasy Ball Park Community. You all probably know it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s where they decided to have a Grimmett get-together. We did get together, I showed up a little late. My daughter said, “Daddy! Y’know him?” When I looked, it was Mack. “Yeah, I know him!” I said. “See! I know all your uncles,” Diane said to her. They were eating, so when I got my food, I went to where Mack was. We were talking all afternoon, remembering things. Two of my brothers that aren’t living, Mack didn’t know, he thought they were still living. He asked me, “Where’s that one? Where’s that one?” – “They died a long time ago,” I told him. “Mmm! I didn’t know,” he said. Rufus, his name was Ulogil(i). “But, Ulogil(i), I went there,” he said. That was the last time I had seen him. Then later, I heard he was in a nursing home at Sallisaw. Before I went to visit him, I heard that he had passed.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t remember him.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah! Me too, he didn’t live that long, right?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, not that long. … Mack Brewer.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah! I know them well. Mack Brewer. Him and my dad were good friends. That place called Oklahoma Smith Furniture Factory, didn’t he work there for a long time?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Me, I worked at Wards Furniture Company.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, me too. It was there, where he worked last. Oklahoma Smith Furniture Factory. They made baby cribs.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, you probably was working there when I was. But I don’t remember what year it was.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, the last job my dad worked let’s see… it was around ’86 he worked last, in Ft. Smith. Then he got sick and had to quit working. When he retired he had worked 44 or 45 years there. Yeah, I think he did the same, Mack Brewer, I think he worked there that long, too. He worked in the Mill Room. And my dad worked downstairs, where they called the “Mattress Room.” He worked there for a long time.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: What they call, Cedar Chests. Or chest drawers, we made those. Me, where I was working, right at the beginning, they were making them and they were just going and going. It didn’t take long to make them.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Who was the boss back then?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Jimmy Barnes.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Jim Barnes…Jim Barnes.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: What’s it called…? The road in Sallisaw.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: 59 Hwy?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Past that lumber yard, what’s that community called?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Rock Pointe?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Past that… that’s where it was … Brushy!
Oh!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Brushy, yeah, yeah. Where I worked at last, the Cabinet Department, the boss there was Roy… Gah, I lost his name. Roy… Haw! I’ll remember after a while.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what happens to me, too!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I know someone real well, then I’ll forget their name.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You remember their name, and then all of a sudden you forget.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Here a while back, my daughter’s husband, Raymond Sanders is his name. That’s who I forgot. It bothers me when that happens. “My daughter’s husband,” I thought, “What is his name?”
[laughter]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Then I remember it. Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That will happen to you.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Tell me again, one more time, what was your name?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mitch Holcomb -- Holcomb.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Mitch?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, that was Ray’s mom, used to be Holcomb. Wasn’t she?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: She was a Pigeon. Pigeon.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: She was a Pigeon? Oh.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: She … it was her, my grandmother (on my dad’s side) she got together with somebody named Holcomb. Some of the Holcombs come from Bunch. Now, we are kin to the Bunch.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s interesting, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: John Bunch.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They are all Bunch.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, we’re kinfolk. Without even knowing it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s how it goes.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. It’s bad. I would like to be acquainted with the ones that live over there. Bunch and Chuculate.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m kin to the Chuculates, too. My grandmother was a Chuculate. Momma’s mom.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: [To himself] Who were the other ones?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ulutse is what they called her, she was a Chuculate.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Ulutse.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: See, like her, I had forgotten all about her, I just now remembered. Ulutse.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Her dad was a Chuculate and her mom was a Weavel. The Weavels, my grandfather’s dad was Muskrat. Weavels and Muskrats we say. [laughs]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: One Muskrat, “Five-O” we call him. He’s terminally ill.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s a preacher, isn’t he?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What is wrong with him?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Just yesterday, somebody told me he’s got stomach cancer.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Ooh wee.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: They said he’s not sleeping, he’s in too much pain.
Oh!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: He would go way off. Far away. He’s just a boy, he’s not really grown.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh-uh. I’d say he’s about 45 years old.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Probably older.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You think so?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Maybe like 58.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s really that old? I really thought he was in his 40s.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Five-O. [To himself] Who was telling me? Me, when I heard he was sick, I called him. He was still talking good. “I’m at Hastings,” he said. They couldn’t find what was wrong with him until it was too late. The same thing happened to my late wife. “Go to the doctor,” we’d tell her. “Huh-uh, it’s gonna be alright,” she’d say. It wasn’t until she was real bad, we took her. It was too late, they said, she had Stage 4 colon cancer and liver. She was eating real good, you wouldn’t believe she was that sick. Then all of a sudden--

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She quit.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: She quit eating, she wasn’t hungry, and she didn’t last long after that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Cancer is real dangerous.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: September 27th, 9:15 am on a Sunday morning, when she left. I still remember real well.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How long were you two married?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: 42 years.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How about where you worked? Where was it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Ft. Smith. Those high-lines, where they spray below. Then Stilwell Foods. And then the last was Facet. I worked at four places in all my life. Just four different places. Then I retired at Facet after 26 years of working there. I lived across the road. I could just walk to work.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So you were able to walk to work? What did you do there?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I was a forklift operator.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Your job was just right there, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: It was also where people got commodities. There was a boy working with us, he heard about how they were going to build a commodity place there. “Hey, Roy,” he said. “We’ve got it made,” he said. “What do you mean?” I said. “All we have to do is bring a fork and a spoon!” [laughter] “What for?” – “Cause there’s gonna be a commodity house across the street!” he said. [laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that what you did?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: You two. This is what I like; to talk our language and to hear someone speaking. Here a while back, I went to visit Mack Flute. For a long time, all afternoon, it was warm outside. We sat on his porch and talked about a lot of things. “Roy, nowadays it’s lonely,” he said. “I sit here by myself all the time. There’s nobody that’ll come and talk to me like we are doing,” he said. “Yeah, I know what you mean. Cause I’m in the same situation,” [I said.]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My dad is the same, too.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Like, when you talk to the drug-users, they don’t really know anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Also, they don’t know what they’re saying.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no, no. Because this next week I was thinking about y’all, I guess I’m feeling better, I can go visit Ama Agasga. That’s his name, her dad. “I can go visit Ama Agasga,” I thought, sitting outside.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He would like that if you come visit him.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Because he can’t walk very well. He can walk a little bit, then has to sit down. That’s why he was riding that scooter when we were looking around.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: His talking is still the same, though?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Tsugalvd(i) – He’s goofy.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s what I’m thinking. He’s probably the only one still here from the ones that used to play ball at Greasy. He’s the only one I can think of.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I think he is the only one.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Greasy baseball players that used to be. That’s what I was thinking. Ama Agasga is the only one still here. That’s what I think, I don’t know. I could be mistaken.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mm!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Y’all were real good ballplayers back then, right?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Really! … My uncle, that I mentioned, he used to live around Marble [City] and Flute Springs area. Galisgwewi was what they called him. He was hard-of-hearing. They used to come visit us. Then one time, he came and told his brothers he was gonna stay with them. “Mm!” they said. So he stayed there a long time. We would sit in the shade in the summer, and I would listen to him tell stories of what it was like when he was young, growing up. What was going to happen – “The Future,” what he knew, he told me. I’ve seen a lot of what he said, but there’s still some I haven’t seen. He used to say, “This is going to happen, this is going to be this way.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some of them really knew, didn’t they?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Nowadays, we don’t know anything.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Nothing! [laughs] We are really living in dangerous times.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And, “They are going to be making a lot more roads and also building more houses,” he said. Now, that is going on all over Stilwell. All that he said is happening. When I go by, I think about it. They are building and have “roadblock” or “detour.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They really are building everywhere.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “That’s what’s going to happen,” they said.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And also, I don’t know if y’all ever been over at the late Asin Thompson’s place? Where she lived at, they made it into a UKB office. I don’t know if you all remember. 100 Hwy, across the road from Stilwell High School.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, yeah!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That used to be a rock building, but they tore it all down. Now, it’s a big, new building there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Wasn’t it where they were taking care of babies?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah. The building wasn’t very good when he came, he lived on 51 Hwy. Then he built another big building there. That Wilson Jr.?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: He said he has been there before. Boy, you would think somebody rich is living there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s true! I’ve been there before, too.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Wilson told me that they’ve put in a pool there, too. When he passed away, I was also really sick with Covid-19. I didn’t go to Asin’s funeral.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where? Wasn’t he laid up at Fayetteville Nursing Home?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, he was a veteran.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I see John Bunch very seldom.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You see him sometimes. You do know where he lives. He lives in a big house, too.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, boy, he does live in a good house.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Didn’t he sell his parents’ land?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Some of it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t think anyone lives there.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Rosie … her grandkids lived there last time I knew.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Did you hear that Rosie has passed?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh, I heard it.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Me, I didn’t hear about it until a month after. I didn’t know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It’s been a long time since I’ve seen her. Probably about 40 years, since I saw her. Leslie is the one who told me.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: How about you? How old are you?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And you?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ll be 62 in February.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: How old do you all think I am?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: 40? [laughs]

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Oh!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: You talked about someone, that should be about the same age. Uh…75?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: …nine.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, you said that earlier, when you were born in ‘44. My mother was born in the same year.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: It won’t be long, if I’m still around, I’ll be 80. I didn’t think I would live that long.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Your mind seems well.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s what they tell me, “You seem well.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: When somebody tells me, “You still look like a young man!” My wife didn’t like it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How about what they call “hobbies,” what do you like to do?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Games?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Hobbies. You might like to do something or make something? Also, paint something?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Oh! Slingshots.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, you make those?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, I’ve got three pairs of them. I’m not bragging. Nobody can beat me either. I’m the best.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Are you talking about a bow?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: They call them “bean-flick.” That rubber, it is hard to find now. When they throw something up, I can hit it. All summer, I’ll sit on my porch and shoot rocks with it. I was sitting there, had my rocks, and a bird way down at the corner, on a post. I didn’t see the bird, I shot one of the rocks that way and [thump] it went. “Why did it sound like that?” I thought I had hit the post. I got up and went to check it out, and there was a woodpecker laying on its back there. That’s what I had hit.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Gah! What do they call them in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Is it Dalala?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, Dalala.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Dalala.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Woodpecker?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah. Also, that big Gwog(i), they call it.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Kog(i)?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: All I’ve heard is Gwog(i). That’s all they’d say, that’s all I’d hear.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about medicine? The kind they go get in the woods, you didn’t learn anything about those?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: For coughing or fever for children, Nok(i)datl(i) they called it. Sagebrush – Nok(i)datl(i). When you break it open, it smells real good. Where the Bunch Bridge is, across the tracks, that’s where so-and-so lives, that Jack Holloway’s widow, what was her name?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Virginia.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Virginia! That’s where she got this stuff, before we would get there, she would take it – Nok(i)datl(i).

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that where you just drink it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, you make it short. You put it into a bundle and tie it off. Then you boil it. It’s good to drink.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about Sassafras, does it just sprout? I mean, where do you find it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It grows all over alongside the road.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Kan(a)sdats(i) they call it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Do you all know there’s two kinds? White and red.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They say the red is the best.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: The reason why I know, somebody taught me. I went to look for it, Kan(a)sdats(i) and found it. I took the roots off and cleaned it up. “Boy, it was good to drink,” that’s what I was telling. “Was it really Kan(a)sdats(i)?” he asked me. “Yeah, it was,” I said. “Was it red?” he asked. “Huh-uh, it wasn’t red,” I told him. “It’s a different Sassafras, there’s two kinds,” he said. “That’s why it wasn’t any good. You picked the white one,” he said. They say it’s good for the blood, Kan(a)sdats(i).

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what they were saying, we were talking to some people and they said the red was better.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Also, headaches.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Kan(a)sdats(i)?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: No! Huh-uh! It’s cherry. Do you know it? Cherry. If you take a branch of that, about this [gestures] long. Do it like this [gestures] and when you have a good pile, put it on a white cloth, cover it good, then tie it up. Put it in water and make it wet, put it on your forehead with a bandana. Boy, it’s good for a headache. And then – are we talking too long?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Huh-uh!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Speak!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Also, Yellow Wood, I don’t know what they call it in English. Ad(a) Didalonige.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Isn’t it Bois d’Arc? They make bows out of it.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: It’s real easy to break. When you do, it’s real yellow. That is good for kidney stones. I know, because I used it. All you have to do is boil it. Just cut them into little sticks, put them in a bundle and boil it. It’s almost just like a tea. One time, a real bad pain started. I couldn’t be still, or even lie down, or even sit down. But finally, they took me to the doctor. They checked me over and even took pictures [X-rays]. That’s what they said it was, “You got five kidney stones. One is right close to your liver.” -- That’s all they did, they said, “We’re gonna send you an appointment.” – I had to go home, but I already knew they were gonna tell me to go home. But I already knew what somebody had taught me. “When I get home, --” I thought. “-- come morning, I’m gonna go get some and fix it.” The morning came, and I had to go work at Facet, but I didn’t go. I knew where it was, the Yellow Wood. I went and got it. Me and my wife boiled some and I started drinking it. The next day, I drank two cups of coffee in the morning, one in the afternoon, and two before I went to bed at night. I did it for five weeks, and it wasn’t hurting. The pain was gone. When I got the letter [for my appointment], nothing was wrong with me, already. So, I didn’t go to the appointment they sent me. Then, me and another man were talking about this medicine. That’s what he mentioned, Yellow Wood, what I’m telling y’all. He had a rock, a stone, that they took out of him. Just to check it out, he put the medicine in a quart jar with water, and put his stone in there. He forgot about it, until way after a while, he said, “I wonder what happened to that rock.” When he checked, it was smaller. So he put it back in the water again. So, when he checked it way after a while, there was nothing. There was no rock in there. That’s what happened.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what happened when you were using that medicine, right?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, it dissolved. Y’all should remember that [this medicine]. Kidney.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Do you know what this medicine is called in English? Is it Yellow Wood, or?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s all I call it. Just Yellow Wood.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ve never heard of it.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Some of them… I’ve heard them call it “ad(a) dalon(i),” they’d say. I don’t know if it’s different from what you’re talking about. But, if someone’s got diabetes, they use that [on themselves].

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s what my wife knew about. “Dalon(i) Usdi” and “Dalon(i) Utan(a).” There were two different kinds, but I didn’t know.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Mm!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ve heard of that, “Dalon(i)” you’re saying. But I don’t know how they used it, was it diabetes you said?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Uh, that “ad(a) dalon(i)” was diabetes. And that “Dalon(i)” was gallbladder. The one that is real painful. That’s what they used back then. My dad used it. Boy, I forget what it looked like, because it was a long time ago. The last time he had pain, they took out his gallbladder.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Mhm. But me too, they had to take my gallbladder out. When they took it out, they said it was all dried up. That’s what happened, drinking that medicine.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It dried it up?!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: It dried up. “It’s dried up,” said the doctor. “I don’t know why it was bothering you!”

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What did you tell him then?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was that medicine that you were drinking, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, it was!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It healed you.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, it healed me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Wow. Well, we’re finishing up now.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I was telling you about Dennis talking on the radio, Sunday mornings. He talks about them having a Cherokee Speakers meeting. I’m wanting to go to it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Isn’t it on the Thursday?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I can check here in a little bit and let you know.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: “It’s good to attend, you’ll like it,” Dennis says.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Dennis is just right in here. Just right here, in the next room.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: This Dennis, before, I had only heard of him. Over here at Walmart, I was looking at clothes. Then a man came on the other side, he was doing the same. Sometimes I’d catch him looking at me. “Who is that? He probably thinks he knows me,” I thought. We kinda greeted each other, “Siyo,” I said. “Siyo,” he said. He started talking – “What’s your name?” I said. That’s what he said, “Dennis Sixkiller.” – “Oh! You talk on the radio.” – “Yeah, yeah.” We stood there for a while talking. That’s when we got acquainted.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s a good guy, Dennis.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: “Come over and speak Cherokee,” he told me. But I haven’t, yet.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, he’s just right in there, right?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, he’s in there.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: “When I make up my mind, I’ll be there,” I told him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What about this Cherokee we’re speaking? What do you think is going to happen to it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Me, I think, just like we are talking now. Talking about things, I think they’re not talking as much and it’s going to stay the same. I was telling them, “When us older ones pass away, a lot of this language is going to disappear.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: I’m going to tell something, I don’t know if it’s something – I don’t want to hurt nobody’s feelings. The politicians in Washington, they are taking everything away from us. Even our language. We were just talking about how children don’t know how to speak it. It’s already happened. When I was growing up, the horses and also the mules, with wagons, they used to be parked at Bunch, when I grew up. It wasn’t even lonesome, there was a railroad track there. They were working on it, some of them were loading up railroad ties, and some were dropping them off. Nowadays, when you see a wagon, it belongs to a white person, and when you see horses, they belong to a white person. Indians, we do not have anything. Even land they have taken away. When I was growing up, my grandmother had a lot of land. When she got ill, she would say, “Go sell this land, they’ll help you.” That’s what they were telling people, and they really believed it. They sold it all, just so they could be getting help. Lits(i) did the same, you knew her, Lits(i) Beaver?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: She was the same.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who was buying the land? Just anybody?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Yeah, anybody.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Anyone who wanted it? … I think that’s what I’ve heard, they had to sell the land they had, then they would start getting checks.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: You know that Gadon(a) […] – She was one of our grandmothers. One of our grandmothers, she left a lot of land. Today, they have about sold it all. But, we weren’t included in any of it. I don’t know what they’re doing, they’re lying – lying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They didn’t use it?

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Where I grew up, I talked about, where we lived, did they sell it? Jimmy Vann. Dirt-Thrower’s son, they said he bought it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mhm.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: How about Betsy? Betsy Bunch. She came to the house. “Have you heard?” she said. “Huh-uh. I don’t know anything,” I told her. “They are selling a lot of land, and they are making a lot of money for themselves,” she said. Those of us others that are still around, and we are still here, too, they haven’t included us at all. They’re doing wrong.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: “Wasn’t she our grandmother?” I think. Ol’ Ryn, that’s passed, Ryn Turner. He used to say—Ryn would say whatever was on his mind.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember him.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: “He really isn’t worth anything,” he used to say.
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The bus driver, her name was Mel(i). She was my friend.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: How about they were talking, I think it was Rainwater that was talking. “Someone’s driving the bus,” he said. “He knows you. He was saying something, but he’s got a short neck. – I saw him,” said Rainwater. “Oh, was it Turner?” – “Yeah!”
[laughter]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember that, Daddy had a short neck. Alright, we’re done!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: That’s where we used to stop by. Those boys, they were drinking some beer at the house. Then they’ll say, “Let’s go visit Rainwater.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mm. I remember that all the time.

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: And your mom would cook. She’d tell the boys they were gonna eat before they went home. Nowadays, people would just run you off!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right, today!

segments.speaker: roy-grimmett
segments.translation: Well, I really enjoyed it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, we did, too.
